structures.title: The basic declarative statement
structures.explanation: French follows a subject-verb-object order like English. The verb agrees with the subject in person and number, and any article on the object must match its gender. This is the neutral order for stating facts.
structures.ex1_ref: I eat / am eating an apple.
structures.ex2_ref: Marie is reading an interesting book.

structures.title: Forming a yes/no question
structures.explanation: Put est-ce que in front of a normal statement to turn it into a question, without changing the word order. It is the everyday middle-register way to ask, less formal than inversion but clearer than intonation alone. Est-ce que becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel.

structures.title: The formal question by inversion
structures.explanation: Invert the verb and subject pronoun, joining them with a hyphen, to form a formal or written question. When the verb ends in a vowel and the subject is il/elle/on, insert -t- for euphony. Question words go first: Où habite-t-il ?

structures.title: Making a sentence negative
structures.explanation: Negation wraps around the conjugated verb with ne before and pas after. Ne shortens to n' before a vowel or mute h. In the passé composé, ne … pas surrounds the auxiliary (n'ai pas mangé).

structures.title: The near future (futur proche)
structures.explanation: Conjugate aller in the present and follow it with an infinitive to express something about to happen or already planned. It is the most common way to talk about the future in speech, like English 'going to'.
structures.ex2_ref: We're going to eat at the restaurant.

structures.title: Emphasizing an action in progress
structures.explanation: Use être en train de + infinitive to stress that an action is happening right at this moment, since French has no separate continuous tense. It corresponds to the English 'to be in the middle of doing'.
structures.ex1_target: Je suis en train de travailler.
structures.ex1_ref: I am (in the middle of) working.
structures.ex2_target: Ils sont en train de dîner.
structures.ex2_ref: They are having dinner right now.

structures.title: Saying there is / there are
structures.explanation: Il y a is an invariable expression meaning both 'there is' and 'there are'; it never changes for number. It states the existence or presence of something. With a time expression it also means 'ago'.
structures.ex2_target: Il y a beaucoup de gens ici.
structures.ex2_ref: There are a lot of people here.

structures.title: Identifying or presenting someone/something
structures.explanation: Use c'est with a singular noun and ce sont with a plural noun to identify or introduce. Prefer c'est (not il/elle est) before an article + noun. In casual speech c'est is often kept even for plurals.

structures.title: An action still going on since the past
structures.explanation: French uses the present tense with depuis for an action that began in the past and continues now, where English uses the present perfect. Depuis marks either a duration ('for') or a starting point ('since').
structures.ex1_target: J'habite à Paris depuis trois ans.
structures.ex1_ref: I have been living in Paris for three years.
structures.ex2_target: Elle apprend le français depuis janvier.
structures.ex2_ref: She has been learning French since January.

structures.title: Linking two verbs with the right preposition
structures.explanation: Many verbs need a fixed preposition before a following infinitive: commencer à, réussir à, apprendre à take à; essayer de, décider de, oublier de take de. The preposition must be memorized with the verb.

structures.title: Comparing two things
structures.explanation: Build a comparison with plus (more), moins (less) or aussi (as) before the adjective and que after it. The adjective still agrees with the noun it describes. Bon becomes meilleur, not plus bon.
structures.ex1_target: Elle est plus grande que moi.
structures.ex1_ref: She is taller than I am.
structures.ex2_target: Ce livre est aussi intéressant que l'autre.
structures.ex2_ref: This book is as interesting as the other one.

structures.title: Obligation, ability and desire
structures.explanation: These three modal verbs are conjugated and followed directly by an infinitive: devoir (must/have to), pouvoir (can/be able to), vouloir (want). No preposition comes between the modal and the infinitive.
structures.ex1_ref: I have to work this weekend.
structures.ex2_target: Est-ce que je peux vous aider ?

structures.title: Joining clauses with a relative pronoun
structures.explanation: Qui is the subject of the relative clause and is followed by a verb; que is the direct object and is followed by a subject + verb. Que elides to qu' before a vowel, but qui never changes.
structures.ex1_target: L'homme qui habite ici est médecin.
structures.ex1_ref: The man who lives here is a doctor.
structures.ex2_target: Le livre que je lis est passionnant.
structures.ex2_ref: The book that I'm reading is fascinating.

structures.title: The real (first) conditional
structures.explanation: For a realistic condition, use si + present tense in the 'if' clause and the futur simple in the result clause. Never put a future or conditional verb directly after si. The clauses can come in either order.
structures.ex1_target: Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai.
structures.ex1_ref: If I have time, I will come.
structures.ex2_ref: If you study, you will succeed.

structures.title: Expressing necessity
structures.explanation: Il faut que is followed by a subject in the subjunctive to say that something is necessary. The subjunctive is required because a personal necessity is imposed on the subject. For a general necessity, il faut + infinitive is enough.
structures.ex1_target: Il faut que tu partes maintenant.
structures.ex2_target: Il faut que nous soyons à l'heure.

structures.title: Expressing purpose (in order to)
structures.explanation: Pour + infinitive states the goal or purpose of an action, answering 'why?' or 'what for?'. Both verbs share the same subject. It corresponds to English 'in order to' or simply 'to'.
structures.ex1_target: J'apprends le français pour travailler à Paris.
structures.ex1_ref: I'm learning French in order to work in Paris.
structures.ex2_target: Elle économise pour acheter une maison.
structures.ex2_ref: She's saving up to buy a house.
